study.title: 2 Kings 14 - Amaziah, Joash, and Jeroboam II: partial zeal, pride, and faithfulness of God
study.overview: The chapter shows two kingdoms in parallel. In Judah, Amaziah begins with a relatively correct reign before the LORD, but his obedience is incomplete: he does not remove the highs, avenges his father's death without exceeding the limit of the law, overcomes Edom, but then enempts and provokes an unnecessary war against Israel. This arrogance ends in defeat, humiliation, loss of wealth, and ultimately death by conspiracy. In Israel, Joash dies, and Jeroboam II succeeds him; although he does what is evil, the text highlights that the LORD used his reign to save Israel from affliction and restore his borders, showing mercy despite the unfaithfulness of the people.

outline.title: The beginning of Amaziah: partial fidelity
outline.explanation: Amaziah ascends the throne in Judah and receives a positive but limited assessment. He does what is right in the eyes of the LORD, but not with the same integrity associated with David. The chapter already signals the problem: the high ones remain active, and the people still participate in undue religious practices.

outline.title: Justice, victory and the fall for pride
outline.explanation: After consolidating his power, Amaziah punishes his father's murderers, but respects the law by not killing their children. Then win Edom and takes Sela. But success leads him to pride: he defies Joash of Israel, receives a parable-shaped answer which denounces his arrogance, and by ignoring it, causes ruin and that of Judah.

outline.title: Death of Joash, humiliation of Amaziah and new phase in Judah
outline.explanation: Joash of Israel dies and is succeeded by Jeroboam. Amaziah survives fifteen more years, but his defeat weakens his government until a conspiracy forces him to flee to Laquis, where he is killed. Then the people of Judah make king Azariah, who recovers Elath for Judah, indicating continuity, despite the crisis.

outline.title: Jeroboam II: prosperity without repentance
outline.explanation: Jeroboam II reigns long in Israel and remains in the sins connected with Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Still, the LORD restores borders and saves Israel through him, not because Israel has been faithful, but for compassion in the face of their affliction and for fidelity to his promise. The chapter ends with the succession by Zechariah.

study.context: The chapter follows the succession of the kings of Judah and Israel. The notes show that Amaziah reigned in Judah and that his rule included a co-regency with his son, Azariah, according to Tyndale's observation. The text also records the continuity of the dynasty in Israel, with Joash being succeeded by Jeroboam II and, in the end, by Zechariah. The historical emphasis of the chapter is not only chronological: it serves to show how God rules in the midst of righteous reigns only in part, evil reigns, and conflicts between the two kingdoms.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that an external religious assessment is not enough: Amaziah does what is correct, but not with the integrity of David, and his tolerance to the high ones reveals incomplete obedience. It also shows that righteousness must remain under the law of God, for he punishes his father's murderers without overcoming the commandment on personal responsibility. Military victory does not confirm spiritual fidelity; on the contrary, success can feed pride and produce a fall. Joash's parable emphasizes that pride leads to destruction. At the same time, the text highlights God's merciful sovereignty: even when Israel remains in sin, the LORD frees him from affliction and restores borders, revealing fidelity to his covenant and compassion before the weakness of the people.

scholarViews.insight: Amaziah received a satisfactory spiritual assessment, but did not serve the Lord with all his heart as David; moreover, the permanence of the highs remained a stumbling block for Judah.
Amaziah began well, but he did not persevere; to do what is certain is not enough if obedience is not maintained with sincerity and resolution before God.
The expression of Joash's second year should be understood as the beginning of the independent government of Amaziah, after a prior association in the kingdom.

questions: In which areas my obedience to God is only partial, as that of Amaziah, and not whole as He requires?
When I receive any victory or recognition, does this lead me to humility or pride that makes me hasty decisions?
How can I trust in God's faithfulness even when I see leaders and people around acting unfaithfully?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine his own fidelity with sincerity. It is not enough to start well; one must persevere in obedience, abandon that which competes with true worship and resist pride after victories. In practice, this means evaluating habits, choices and motivations before God, repent of all excessive trust in yourself and seek prudent decisions rather than provocation and self-confidence. It also encourages resting in the mercy of God, who continues to act despite human weakness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify all the chronological details nor allow to safely develop broader historical reconstructions. Tyndale's reference to possible co-regenerities should be treated as an auxiliary interpretation, not as absolute certainty from this chapter. It is also not possible to safely determine, only with this material, all the political motives involved in the dispute between Amaziah and Joas, in addition to what the text explicitly reports.
